newsitem.title: USA: Harrah's passes New Orleans casino hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Harrah's passes New Orleans casino hurdle.

text.p: Harrah's Jazz Co cleared another major hurdle Tuesday in its efforts to resurrect Louisiana's only land-based casino, which has been mired in bankruptcy proceedings since November 1995.

Late Tuesday, the Louisiana Gaming Control Commission unanimously approved the operating agreement with the state, one day after a federal bankruptcy court judge confirmed the Harrah's Jazz plan for reorganization, board spokeswoman Lana Tramonge told Reuters.
The confirmation on Monday let Harrah's emerge from bankruptcy protection, subject to approval by the Gaming Commission, the governor, the legislature and New Orleans' City Council.
Tramonge said the city council already has signed off on the plan, which goes next to Gov. Mike Foster and then the legislature.
In negotiations on the bankruptcy reorganization, Foster refused to compromise on monies owed to the state in its original contract with Harrah's, including $100 million annual payments.

Harrah's spokesman Ralph Berry said construction could be completed on the massive casino adjacent to the historic French Quarter within 10 months. If all parties agree to the plan, the casino could open in spring 1998.

Under the reorganization plan, the casino company will emerge as a new company called Jazz Casino Co. In exchange for their $435 million in junk bond debt, bondholders will recieve $187 million in new bonds and slightly more than 50 percent of the new company's stock.
Forty percent of the remaining ownership will be controlled by Harrah's Entertainment Inc, and a group of private investors will control the rest.
Unsecured creditors, the largest of which is general contractor Centex-Landis, will be paid in full for claims totaling about $105 million.
The reorganization plan calls for a casino with 100,000 square feet of gambling space, half of the 200,000 square feet originally planned.
